# WebMCP

[WebMCP](https://github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp) lets a web page offer tools to an AI agent
that works in the reader's browser. Instead of reading the screen, the agent calls a tool such as
`search_docs` and gets back structured results. With WebMCP turned on, every page of a Great Docs
site registers a small set of read-only tools for finding and reading the site's documentation. In
browsers without WebMCP, nothing visible changes.

This complements the files Great Docs already writes for agents that fetch content directly, such
as [`llms.txt`](39-llms-txt.qmd) and [Agent Skills](38-agent-skills.qmd). WebMCP serves agents that
are in the tab with the reader.

::: {.callout-warning}
## This feature is experimental

WebMCP is a proposed web standard from the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group, and the
browser API is still changing. Great Docs' support is off by default, and the tools and their
results may change in future releases. If something doesn't work as described here, please [open
an issue](https://github.com/posit-dev/great-docs/issues).
:::

## Browser Support

Chrome 149 and later support WebMCP behind a flag: turn on `chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing`
(or start Chrome with `--enable-features=WebMCP`). Stable Chrome doesn't turn it on by default yet,
and other browsers don't support it.

Tools register on `https://` sites and on `localhost`. A page embedded in a cross-origin `<iframe>`
registers no tools unless the embedding page allows it through the `tools` Permissions Policy.

## Turning It On

Add `webmcp: true` to `great-docs.yml`:

```{.yaml filename="docs/great-docs.yml"}
webmcp: true
```

The next build then:

- adds the WebMCP runtime, `webmcp.js`, to every page
- writes `gd-webmcp.json` at the site root, a manifest of the site's sections, pages and API names
  that the tools read
- adds a "WebMCP tools" section to `llms.txt`, so agents that read the file learn about the tools

The runtime loads nothing until a tool is called. Each tool fetches the files it needs, such as
the manifest, a page's Markdown companion or Quarto's search index, and keeps them for later calls.

A [versioned site](30-multi-version-docs.qmd) gets a manifest for each version, and the tools on a
page read the manifest of that page's version.

## Trying It Locally

To see the tools in action:

1. Turn on `chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing` and restart Chrome.
2. Install Chrome's **Model Context Tool Inspector** extension, which lists a page's tools and lets
   you call them by hand.
3. Build the site with `webmcp: true`, then serve it:

   ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
   great-docs build
   great-docs preview
   ```

4. Open any page and the Inspector. It lists the tools, and you can call one with input such as
   `{"query": "install"}`.

Serve the site rather than opening its HTML files directly. Chrome blocks the requests the tools
make from a `file://` page, so most tools would fail.

## The Tools

Every page registers these five tools, and a site with an API reference adds two more. Each tool's
description tells the agent when to use it and gives an example question.

| Tool | Returns | Example question |
|---|---|---|
| `get_site_overview` | The package's name, description, version, install commands, license and repository; the site's sections; files for agents such as `llms.txt`; the open page; and the tools on the page | "What is this package and how do I install it?" |
| `get_current_page` | The open page as Markdown, or with `format: "outline"`, its headings | "Summarise this page." |
| `list_pages` | The site's pages grouped by section, with titles, URLs, descriptions, tags and status. Blog posts come newest first | "What guides are there?" |
| `get_page` | One page, or one `section` of it, as Markdown. `page` can be a path, URL, title, file name or API name | "Show me the GitHub Pages part of the deployment guide." |
| `search_docs` | The best-matching page sections for a `query`, with excerpts, URLs and scores. `scope` limits the search to one kind of page (such as `guide`, `api` or `blog`) or one section | "How do I deploy to GitHub Pages?" |

The API tools read the API reference:

| Tool | Returns | Example question |
|---|---|---|
| `list_api` | The documented classes, functions and methods grouped by reference section, each with its full name, kind, summary and URL. `section` picks one section by title | "Which functions does this package have?" |
| `get_api_reference` | One object's summary, signature and description, and its docstring sections, such as `parameters`, `returns`, `raises` and `examples`, as Markdown. `include` picks the parts to return, and `"markdown"` adds the whole reference | "What arguments does `spin()` take?" |

`get_api_reference` finds an object by its full name (`pkg.Widget.spin`), a short name (`spin` or
`Widget.spin`) in any case, or the end of its full name. A name that fits more than one object, or
none, comes back as an error listing the closest objects. On an object's reference page, `name` is
optional and defaults to that object.

The docstring sections are named after the reference's headings. On a site in another
[language](23-internationalization.qmd), the headings are translated, so `include` can pick only the
signature, the description and the Markdown. Leave `include` out to get every section.

A few details apply to all of them:

- **Results are JSON objects with absolute URLs**, so an agent can link the reader to what it found.
- **Long pages are cut.** `get_page` and `get_current_page` return at most `max_chars` characters
  (40,000 by default), and a cut page comes with its outline so the agent can ask for one section.
- **Errors come back as results**, never as exceptions, so the agent sees what went wrong. An error
  is `{"error": {"code": ..., "message": ...}}`, with one of these codes: `invalid_input`,
  `not_found`, `ambiguous` (with `candidates` to choose from), `fetch_failed`, `unavailable` or
  `internal`.
- **The Markdown comes from the page's companion `.md` file**, so code blocks and tables arrive
  intact. With [`markdown_pages: false`](05-configuration.qmd#markdown-pages), `get_page` and
  `get_api_reference` can't read pages and report `unavailable` with the page's URL, and
  `get_current_page` falls back to the page's text.

## Calling the Tools from Scripts

The same tools are available to scripts on the page through `window.greatDocs.tools`, in every
browser, whether or not it supports WebMCP. Browser-automation agents and your own scripts can use
them this way:

```js
const result = await window.greatDocs.tools.call("search_docs", { query: "install" });
```

`window.greatDocs.tools` has these members:

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `status` | The registration status, as described under [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) |
| `list()` | Each tool's name, title, description, input schema and annotations |
| `call(name, input)` | Runs a tool and returns a promise of its result. The promise never rejects: failures are error results |
| `add(toolOrTools)` | Registers one tool or an array of tools of your own, returning `{added, rejected}` |

When registration has finished, whatever its status, the runtime fires a `gd-webmcp:ready` event
on `document`, with `window.greatDocs.tools` as the event's `detail`. `window.greatDocs.tools`
itself exists from the moment the runtime starts, so `list()`, `call()` and `add()` work before
then.

### Adding Your Own Tools

A site can register its own tools with `add()`. Each tool needs:

- a `name` of 1 to 128 letters, digits, `_`, `-` or `.`, other than one of Great Docs' tool names
- a `description` that tells the agent when to use the tool
- an `execute` function that returns the result, or a promise of it

A tool can also have a `title`, an `inputSchema` (a JSON Schema with `type: "object"`, against
which the input is checked before `execute` runs) and `annotations`. Set `readOnlyHint: true` for a
tool that only looks things up: agents treat a tool without it as one that may change something.

This example adds a tool through [`include_in_header`](11-theming.qmd#include-in-header). The
script may run before or after the runtime, so it uses `window.greatDocs.tools` if it exists and
otherwise waits for the ready event:

```{.yaml filename="docs/great-docs.yml"}
include_in_header:
  - text: |
      <script>
        function addSupportTool(tools) {
          const { rejected } = tools.add({
            name: "get_support_policy",
            title: "Get the support policy",
            description:
              "Use this when the user asks which Python versions the package supports. " +
              'Example: "Does it work on Python 3.9?"',
            annotations: { readOnlyHint: true },
            execute: () => ({
              python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"],
              url: new URL("user-guide/installation.html", document.baseURI).href,
            }),
          });
          if (rejected.length) console.warn("Tool not added:", rejected);
        }
        if (window.greatDocs?.tools) {
          addSupportTool(window.greatDocs.tools);
        } else {
          document.addEventListener("gd-webmcp:ready", (event) => addSupportTool(event.detail), {
            once: true,
          });
        }
      </script>
```

`add()` runs your tools through the same checks as the built-in ones: input that doesn't match the
schema comes back as an `invalid_input` error, and an `execute` that throws comes back as an
`internal` error. On a page that has opted out of WebMCP, `add()` rejects every tool.

## Options

`webmcp: true` turns the feature on with these defaults. Use a mapping to change them:

```{.yaml filename="docs/great-docs.yml"}
webmcp:
  enabled: true
  actions: true       # Register tools that change the page (none yet)
  js_api: true        # Expose the tools as window.greatDocs.tools
  exclude_tools: []   # Tool names to leave out, such as [search_docs]
  origin_trials: []   # Origin-trial tokens to add to every page
```

- **`actions`**: whether to register tools that change the page rather than read it, such as
  going to another page. Great Docs doesn't have any yet; set this to `false` to keep them off when
  it does.
- **`js_api`**: set this to `false` to keep `window.greatDocs.tools` and the `gd-webmcp:ready`
  event off the page. The tools still register with the browser.
- **`exclude_tools`**: tools to leave out on every page. They're also left out of `llms.txt`. A
  name Great Docs doesn't know produces a warning rather than an error.
- **`origin_trials`**: see [Origin Trials](#origin-trials).

## Leaving Pages Out

To keep a page from registering tools, set `webmcp: false` in its front matter:

```{.yaml filename="user_guide/internal-notes.qmd"}
---
title: Internal Notes
webmcp: false
---
```

To keep the tools working on a page but leave the page out of the manifest, so that `list_pages`,
`get_page` and `search_docs` don't offer it, set `listed: false`:

```{.yaml filename="user_guide/changelog-archive.qmd"}
---
title: Changelog Archive
webmcp:
  listed: false
---
```

Draft pages are always left out of the manifest.

## Origin Trials

Chrome sometimes makes a feature available on stable Chrome, without the flag, through an [origin
trial](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/origin-trials): you register your site's
origin and get a token to put on its pages. If WebMCP has an origin trial, add your token to
`origin_trials`, and Great Docs writes it into every page's `<head>`:

```{.yaml filename="docs/great-docs.yml"}
webmcp:
  enabled: true
  origin_trials:
    - "AqW8...your token..."
```

Tokens are tied to an origin, so a token for your deployed site doesn't work on `localhost`. They
aren't secret.

## Privacy and Security

- **The tools only read what the site already publishes**: its pages, their Markdown companions,
  `search.json` and `gd-webmcp.json`. They don't read cookies or storage, and they only fetch from
  the site's own origin.
- **Every built-in tool is read-only.** The tools are registered with `readOnlyHint: true`, which
  tells agents they don't change anything.
- **Results are data.** Nothing a tool returns is run as code.

## Troubleshooting

The runtime records how registration went in a `data-gd-webmcp` attribute on the `<html>` element,
which you can check in DevTools (and which `window.greatDocs.tools.status` also returns):

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pending` | The tools are still registering |
| `registered` | The browser accepted every tool |
| `partial` | The browser refused some tools; the console says which |
| `failed` | The browser refused every tool, as it does in a cross-origin frame |
| `unavailable` | The browser doesn't support WebMCP. `window.greatDocs.tools` still works |
| `off` | The page has opted out, or `exclude_tools` leaves no tools |

If the attribute is missing, the page doesn't load the runtime: check that the site was built with
`webmcp: true`.

Some other problems and their causes:

- **`list_pages`, `get_page` and `search_docs` report `fetch_failed`, and `get_site_overview` has
  no site details.** The page was probably opened from a `file://` URL, where Chrome blocks the
  requests the tools make. Serve the site with `great-docs preview` instead.
- **`list_api` and `get_api_reference` aren't registered.** The site has no API reference, or
  the build skipped it.
- **`search_docs` reports `fetch_failed` but other tools work.** The site has no `search.json`,
  which Quarto writes when the site has search turned on.
- **A page is missing from `list_pages`.** It's a draft, sets `webmcp: {listed: false}`, or wasn't
  rendered in this build.
